steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Applications" section of the Wikipedia article on cryptographic accumulators: what accumulators have been used for, from timestamping and group membership to other secure data structures and Zerocoin.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Timestamping documents
- Group members recognizing each other later (ID escrow)
- Building other secure data structures
- Zerocoin, Zerocash and Zcash

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Timestamping documents
  - Haber and Stornetta, 1990: accumulators for timestamping via cryptographic chaining
  - anticipates modern cryptographic blockchain
  - Benaloh and de Mare, 1991: alternative scheme, time discretized into rounds
- Group members recognizing each other later
  - Benaloh and de Mare: large group recognize each other at a later time
  - Fazio and Nicolosi call it "ID Escrow"
  - each person picks y = identity; group picks public accumulator h and secret x
  - group publishes/saves hash function + accumulated hash of all identities (w.r.t. x and accumulator)
  - each member keeps own y + accumulated hash of everyone except themselves
  - no mutual trust, or trapdoor (RSA-inspired accumulator) -> secure multiparty computation
  - verification: claimed member presents identity + personal accumulated hash (or zero-knowledge proof); accumulate identity, compare against group hash
  - dynamic accumulator: easy to add/remove members afterward
- Other secure data structures
  - Barić and Pfitzmann: fail-stop signatures in constant space, via compression property
  - Goodrich et al.: size-oblivious, efficient, dynamic authenticated dictionary; untrusted directories give verifiable answers to membership queries
  - Papamanthou et al.: cryptographically secure hash table, authenticated when stored remotely
- Zerocoin and successors
  - renewed interest: Zerocoin add on to bitcoin; removes trackable linkage in blockchain -> anonymous, more private transactions
  - mint: publish coin + commitment to serial number with secret random value; accepted if correctly formatted
  - spend: publish serial number + NIZK proof of knowing a published commitment for it, claim coin; accepted if NIZKP valid and serial number not seen before
  - succeeded by Zerocash; being developed into Zcash, digital currency on Bitcoin's codebase

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In 1990 Haber and Stornetta showed that accumulators can be used for timestamping documents, by using cryptographic chaining. This idea anticipates what we now call a cryptographic blockchain. In 1991 Benaloh and de Mare proposed a different scheme, which is based on discretizing time into rounds.

Benaloh and de Mare also showed that accumulators can be used so that a large group of people can recognize each other later on. Fazio and Nicolosi call this situation "ID Escrow". Each person picks a y that represents their identity, and the group as a whole picks a public accumulator h and a secret x . Then the group publishes or saves the hash function and the accumulated hash of all the identities in the group with respect to the secret x and the public accumulator. At the same time each member keeps its identity value y and also the accumulated hash of all the group's identities except its own. If the people in the large group do not trust each other, or if the accumulator has a cryptographic trapdoor like the RSA-inspired accumulator does, they can compute the accumulated hashes by secure multiparty computation. Later, to verify that a claimed member really did belong to the group, the member presents their identity and their personal accumulated hash, or a zero-knowledge proof of it. Anyone can then verify the member by accumulating the claimed member's identity and checking it against the accumulated hash of the whole group. If a dynamic accumulator scheme is used, it is also easy to add or remove members afterward.

- Other secure data structures
  - Barić and Pfitzmann: fail-stop signatures in constant space, via compression property
  - Goodrich et al.: size-oblivious, efficient, dynamic authenticated dictionary; untrusted directories give verifiable answers to membership queries
  - Papamanthou et al.: cryptographically secure hash table, authenticated when stored remotely
- Zerocoin and successors
  - renewed interest: Zerocoin add on to bitcoin; removes trackable linkage in blockchain -> anonymous, more private transactions
  - mint: publish coin + commitment to serial number with secret random value; accepted if correctly formatted
  - spend: publish serial number + NIZK proof of knowing a published commitment for it, claim coin; accepted if NIZKP valid and serial number not seen before
  - succeeded by Zerocash; being developed into Zcash, digital currency on Bitcoin's codebase

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In 1990 Haber and Stornetta showed that accumulators can be used for timestamping documents, by using cryptographic chaining. This idea anticipates what we now call a cryptographic blockchain. In 1991 Benaloh and de Mare proposed a different scheme, which is based on discretizing time into rounds.

Benaloh and de Mare also showed that accumulators can be used so that a large group of people can recognize each other later on. Fazio and Nicolosi call this situation "ID Escrow". Each person picks a y that represents their identity, and the group as a whole picks a public accumulator h and a secret x . Then the group publishes or saves the hash function and the accumulated hash of all the identities in the group with respect to the secret x and the public accumulator. At the same time each member keeps its identity value y and also the accumulated hash of all the group's identities except its own. If the people in the large group do not trust each other, or if the accumulator has a cryptographic trapdoor like the RSA-inspired accumulator does, they can compute the accumulated hashes by secure multiparty computation. Later, to verify that a claimed member really did belong to the group, the member presents their identity and their personal accumulated hash, or a zero-knowledge proof of it. Anyone can then verify the member by accumulating the claimed member's identity and checking it against the accumulated hash of the whole group. If a dynamic accumulator scheme is used, it is also easy to add or remove members afterward.

Cryptographic accumulators can also be used to build other data structures that are cryptographically secure:

Barić and Pfitzmann show that fail-stop signatures can be constructed with only constant space by exploiting the compression property.

Goodrich et al. constructed a dynamic authenticated dictionary that is size-oblivious and efficient. It lets untrusted directories give answers to membership queries that can be cryptographically verified.

Papamanthou et al. constructed a cryptographically secure hash table, and its functionality can be authenticated when it is stored remotely.

There has been renewed interest in the concept because of Zerocoin, an add on to bitcoin. Zerocoin uses cryptographic accumulators to get rid of trackable linkage in the bitcoin blockchain, which would make transactions anonymous and more private. To mint (create) a Zerocoin, someone publishes a coin and a cryptographic commitment to a serial number with a secret random value, and all users will accept it as long as it is correctly formatted. To spend (reclaim) a Zerocoin, someone publishes the serial number of the Zerocoin together with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof that they know of some published commitment that relates to the claimed serial number, and then claims the coin. All users will accept this as long as the NIZKP is valid and the serial number has not appeared before. Zerocoin has since been succeeded by the Zerocash protocol, and it is currently being developed into Zcash, a digital currency based on the codebase of Bitcoin.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Haber and Stornetta showed in 1990 that accumulators can be used to timestamp documents through cryptographic chaining. (This concept anticipates the modern notion of a cryptographic blockchain.)[1,2,3] Benaloh and de Mare proposed an alternative scheme in 1991, based on discretizing time into rounds.[1,4]

Benaloh and de Mare showed that accumulators can be used so that a large group of people can recognize each other at a later time (Fazio and Nicolosi call this an "ID Escrow" situation). Each person selects a y representing their identity, and the group collectively selects a public accumulator h and a secret x . Then, the group publishes or saves the hash function and the accumulated hash of all the group's identities w.r.t the secret x and public accumulator; at the same time, each member of the group keeps both its identity value y and the accumulated hash of all the group's identities except its own. (If the large group of people do not trust each other, or if the accumulator has a cryptographic trapdoor as with the RSA-inspired accumulator, they can compute the accumulated hashes by secure multiparty computation.) To verify later that a claimed member did indeed belong to the group, they present their identity and personal accumulated hash (or a zero-knowledge proof of it); by accumulating the identity of the claimed member and checking it against the accumulated hash of the entire group, anyone can verify a member of the group.[1,2] With a dynamic accumulator scheme, it is also easy to add or remove members afterward.[2,5]

Cryptographic accumulators can also be used to construct other cryptographically secure data structures:

Barić and Pfitzmann show that fail-stop signatures can be constructed with only constant space by exploiting the compression property.[2,6]

Goodrich et al. constructed a size-oblivious, efficient, dynamic authenticated dictionary (which lets untrusted directories give cryptographically verifiable answers to membership queries).[2,7]

Papamanthou et al. constructed a cryptographically secure hash table whose functionality can be authenticated when it is stored remotely.[8]

The concept has received renewed interest because of the Zerocoin add on to bitcoin, which uses cryptographic accumulators to eliminate trackable linkage in the bitcoin blockchain, making transactions anonymous and more private.[9,10,11] More concretely, to mint (create) a Zerocoin, one publishes a coin and a cryptographic commitment to a serial number with a secret random value (which all users will accept as long as it is correctly formatted); to spend (reclaim) a Zerocoin, one publishes the Zerocoin's serial number along with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof that they know of some published commitment relating to the claimed serial number, then claims the coin (which all users will accept as long as the NIZKP is valid and the serial number has not appeared before).[9,10] Since the initial proposal, Zerocoin has been succeeded by the Zerocash protocol and is currently being developed into Zcash, a digital currency based on Bitcoin's codebase.[12,13]
